# Audio

## Two setup rules

```js
import { audio, loader } from "melonjs";

audio.init("mp3,ogg");                      // 1. BEFORE preloading any audio

await loader.preload([
    { name: "cling", type: "audio", src: "data/sfx/" },   // 2. a PREFIX, not a file
]);
```

1. **`audio.init(format)` must run before any audio asset is preloaded**, and
   lists the formats you actually ship. Preloading first fails the preload:
   `await loader.preload(...)` rejects with the loader's `Failed loading
   resource <src>`, which hides the real reason, `target audio extension(s)
   should be set through me.audio.init() before calling the preloader.`
   (thrown as it is by `audio.load()` called directly). It returns `false`
   when no audio backend is available, so it is worth checking. The format
   list defaults to `"mp3"`.
2. **`src` is a prefix, not a file.** The loader appends the asset `name` plus
   each configured extension and uses the first that loads — so
   `data/sfx/` + `cling` + `mp3` → `data/sfx/cling.mp3`. Passing a full filename
   gives you a 404. A `data:audio/...` URL is the one exception: it is used
   verbatim, prefix and extension skipped.

`audio.hasAudio()` says whether the browser can play audio at all, and
`audio.hasFormat("ogg")` whether it can play one codec — useful for choosing
the `init` list or hiding a sound toggle on a device with no audio.

Order matters — melonJS tries the listed formats left to right, so put the
preferred one first. Two formats (`"webm,mp3"` or `"mp3,ogg"`) is the usual
belt-and-braces for codec coverage. Accepted tokens: `mp3`, `mpeg`, `opus`,
`ogg`, `oga`, `wav`, `aac`, `caf`, `m4a`, `m4b`, `mp4`, `weba`, `webm`, `dolby`,
`flac`.

## Effects versus music

```js
audio.play("cling");                    // fire and forget
audio.play("cling", false, null, 0.5);  // loop, onend, volume
const id = audio.play("engine", true);  // looping; keep the id to stop it

audio.playTrack("theme");               // background music
audio.stopTrack();
```

Use **`playTrack`** for music, not `play`. `playTrack(name, volume?)` (or
`playTrack(name, { volume, sprite })`, to loop one region of the clip) always
loops, and it records the name as the current track — which is what
`app.pauseOnBlur` / `resumeOnFocus` / `stopOnBlur` act on, via
`state.pause(true)` → `pauseTrack()`. `stopTrack()`, `pauseTrack()`,
`resumeTrack()` and `getCurrentTrack()` all read that same single slot, so there
is only ever one current *track name*.

`playTrack` on a track that is paused restarts it. `pauseTrack` and
`resumeTrack` act on the track alone, so effects played from the same file (an
audio sprite holding both) keep going, and `resumeTrack` on a track that is
playing does nothing.

**`playTrack` stops the track it replaces** (20.9.0 and later; before that it
only assigned the slot, and the previous bed kept looping underneath where
`stopTrack()` could no longer reach it). So a scene just states its own music
and nothing cancels anything:

```js
class PlayScreen extends Stage {
    onResetEvent() { audio.playTrack("battle", 0.6); }
}
```

Calling it with the track already playing **restarts** it, the same as `play()`
on any other clip. A scene that wants the bed to carry on across a screen
change should not call it again, rather than rely on it doing nothing.

`stopTrack()` is for where nothing follows: a scene whose successor has no
music of its own, or a game going quiet. `state.change` destroys the outgoing
stage **before** it resets the incoming one, so a `stopTrack()` in
`onDestroyEvent` and a `playTrack()` in the next `onResetEvent` are in that
order and never cancel each other.

To end a track on an event rather than on a screen change, say a run ending
while the player stays on the same screen, `audio.fade(name, from, 0, ms)`
takes it down gently. A fade to zero is silence, not a stop, so the voice is
still live until something stops it or replaces it.

Every per-clip function throws `audio clip <name> does not exist` if the clip was
never loaded, and `play` additionally throws when a named sprite region is
missing.

## Audio sprites

One file carrying many effects, with named regions in milliseconds:

```js
await loader.preload([{
    name: "sfx", type: "audio", src: "data/sfx/",
    sprite: { jump: [0, 450], hit: [2000, 250], music: [4000, 12000, true] },
}]);

audio.play("sfx", { sprite: "jump" });
```

### A loop with no gap

An MP3 encoder pads the end of its file. Chrome and Firefox trim the padding when
they decode it, Safari keeps it, so a looping MP3 has a short silence at every
loop there (27 ms on a 12 s clip at 22 kHz, measured). Declare a region of the
loop's exact length and loop on that: the voice never reaches the padding.

```js
await loader.preload([{
    name: "ambience", type: "audio", src: "data/sfx/",
    sprite: { loop: [0, 12000] },
}]);
audio.playTrack("ambience", { sprite: "loop", volume: 0.6 });
// or, as a plain clip: audio.play("ambience", { sprite: "loop", loop: true })
```

Ogg Vorbis carries no such padding.

The optional third element marks a region as looping: it loops unless `play()` is
told `loop: false` (before 20.11 it only looped when `loop: true` was passed as
well). `play()`'s second argument
takes either the original `loop` boolean or a `PlayOptions` object
(`sprite`, `loop`, `onend`, `volume`, plus the spatial `follow`, `at` and
`stopWithTarget`) — both forms work. Object fields win over the positional
`onend` / `volume` arguments when both are supplied.

## Clip state

```js
audio.duration("theme");        // seconds — 0 while still loading
audio.duration("sfx", id);      // duration of the region THAT instance plays
audio.playing("theme");         // is anything playing?
audio.playing("theme", id);     // is that instance playing?
audio.state("theme");           // "unloaded" | "loading" | "loaded"
```

`stop()`, `pause()` and `resume()` take an optional instance `id` too; omit it
and the whole group is affected. `audio.stop()` with no arguments at all stops
every sound. `audio.seek(name)` reads the position, `audio.seek(name, s, id?)`
writes it; `audio.rate(name, r, id?)` changes speed and pitch together
(`0.5`..`4.0`, `1` is normal) and `audio.fade(name, from, to, ms, id?)` ramps
the volume (`0`..`1`, over milliseconds).

## Volume and muting

```js
audio.setVolume(0.5);           // global, 0..1
audio.getVolume();              // read it back
audio.mute("cling");            // one clip  — mute(name, id?, shouldMute = true)
audio.unmute("cling");
audio.muteAll();                // everything (audio.disable() is an alias)
audio.unmuteAll();              // (audio.enable() is an alias)
audio.muted();                  // global mute state
```

`setVolume` is a master level over everything; the `volume` given to a `play`
or `playTrack` is that sound's own level, 1 when left out, and what is heard is
the product of the two. So a music slider fades the track's own level
(`audio.fade(name, v, v, 1)`) and a master slider calls `setVolume`.

`audio.unload(name)` / `audio.unloadAll()` free the decoded buffers; `unload`
also clears the current-track pointer if it named that clip.

### Losing focus mutes everything

When the window loses focus the engine mutes all audio, and unmutes it on
focus. That covers sound effects, procedural `tone` / `noise` and the mixer
effects, not just the music track that `state.pause()` pauses. Set
`app.pauseOnBlur = false` (with `stopOnBlur` left at its `false` default) if a
clip has to keep playing in the background. It is a property of the
application, not a constructor setting: `new Application(w, h, { pauseOnBlur:
false })` does nothing.

## Spatial audio

```js
audio.position("engine", x, y, z);
audio.orientation("engine", x, y, z);
audio.stereo("engine", -1);     // -1 left … 1 right
audio.panner("engine", { coneInnerAngle: 90, /* … */ });
```

`position(name, x, y = 0, z = -0.5, id?)` and
`orientation(name, x, y, z, id?)` both default `id` to "the whole group".
Called with just the clip name, each of the four returns the current value —
`stereo` gives `0` and `position` gives `[0, 0, 0]` before they have ever been
set.

### Let the engine place the sound: `follow` and `at`

The shortest path to positional audio is a play option. Both take **world
pixels**, the same numbers as `pos.x` / `pos.y`, and the engine converts to
audio space for you:

```js
// tracks the renderable every frame, and stops when it is destroyed
audio.play("ufo", { follow: this, stopWithTarget: true });

// pinned to a fixed world point
audio.play("portal", { at: { x: 1200, y: 480 } });
```

`follow` and `at` are mutually exclusive: passing both throws, rather than
quietly picking one. `follow` re-reads the target's **absolute** position each
frame, so a renderable nested in a moving container is placed correctly. That
position is where its `anchorPoint` sits: the center of a `Renderable` or a
`Sprite`, but the **top-left corner** of an `Entity` or an object loaded from
Tiled, whose anchor is `(0, 0)`, so a large one (a boss) sounds from up and to
the left of where it looks to be. `stopWithTarget` is what you want for a sound
that belongs to an entity: without it a looping clip on a destroyed renderable
keeps playing from wherever it last was. It also counts a pooled renderable
going back to its pool, which can lend it out again before the next frame.
`audio.unfollow(id)` detaches a sound and leaves it playing where it is.

### Move the listener, don't do the subtraction yourself

```js
audio.setListener(player);                  // tracked every frame
audio.listener(x, y, z);                    // or place it by hand
audio.listener();                           // → [x, y, z] in world pixels
audio.listenerOrientation(fx, fy, fz, ux, uy, uz);
audio.setListener(null);                    // stop tracking
```

With a listener in the world, source positions are **absolute world
coordinates**, not offsets. The older idiom — passing `source.pos.x -
player.pos.x` every frame with the ear stuck at the origin — still works, but
only if you leave the listener at `(0, 0, 0)`; mixing the two double-counts the
player's position.

`setListener` places the ear at the target's absolute position after the world
updates. A plain renderable contributes position only, so a side-scroller keeps
the default "facing into the screen" and gets left-right panning plus distance
falloff from the one call. A `Camera2d` (`audio.setListener(app.viewport)` in a
2D game) is heard from the **center of its view**, its `worldView`, zoom and
offset included, not from its `pos`, the view's top-left corner (before 20.12
it was the corner, and everything panned right). Following stops on its own
when the target is destroyed, which a stage that owns its camera does on every
state change.

A `Camera3d` target also contributes its **orientation**, taken from its own
basis, so turning the camera swings the stereo image with it. That is the whole
of what a posed 3D scene needs:

```js
audio.setListener(app.viewport);                 // in a 3D scene this is a Camera3d
audio.play("drone", { follow: saucer });         // scene coordinates, directly
```

**Y is down.** Every one of these calls takes and returns melonJS world
coordinates, where y grows downward; the Y-up flip Web Audio wants happens
inside the engine. Pass `pos.y` as it is.

### The defaults are tuned for pixels

`audio.setSpatialDefaults()` / `getSpatialDefaults()` set the panner attributes
a sound placed through `follow` or `at` starts from, and the shipped values
assume a 2D game measured in pixels:

| attribute | default |
|---|---|
| `refDistance` | `240` |
| `maxDistance` | `10000` |
| `panningModel` | `"equalpower"` |
| `distanceModel` | `"inverse"` |

With those, a placed sound is at full volume out to 240 px and then halves
each time the distance doubles: about half at 480, a quarter at 960, roughly
an eighth at 2000. `maxDistance` is where it stops getting quieter.

**They apply to placed sounds only.** A plain `audio.play()` followed by a
bare `audio.position()` keeps WebAudio's own defaults, where `refDistance` is
`1` METRE and a source 100 px out is already near silent. That path is
unchanged, which is what keeps old code working.

Widen or tighten the field once, globally:

```js
audio.setSpatialDefaults({ refDistance: 400, maxDistance: 20000 });
```

`audio.panner(name, attrs, id?)` still overrides per clip or per voice, and it
merges over the current values rather than replacing them, so writing one field
no longer resets the rest. Called without an `id` it writes the **group**
defaults, which is what a clip-wide tuning call looks like.

For a 3D scene where front-to-back matters, `panningModel: "HRTF"` is worth the
cost; for a 2D one it mostly muddies the stereo image.

### `stereo` and `position`: last writer wins

Both drive the same per-instance panner node, and the engine swaps the node to
match whichever you called **last**: `stereo()` after `position()` gives you
plain left-right panning, and `position()` after `stereo()` gives you 3D
falloff. Neither silently does nothing any more, and the order you call them in
no longer matters.

Still pick one per voice and stay with it. A 2D game usually wants `stereo()`
alone; reach for `position()` (or `follow` / `at`) when distance falloff
matters.

**Spatial audio is WebAudio-only.** On a clip loaded with `stream: true` (or
`html5: true`, or `preload: false`) `stereo` / `position` / `orientation` return early and do
nothing — which is exactly the case for the long music tracks people reach for
first. `follow` and `at` are equally inert on a streamed clip.

## Procedural sound

For beeps, blips and noise without shipping files. Both take **one options
object**, and `duration` (in seconds) is required:

```js
audio.tone({ freq: 440, duration: 0.2, gain: 0.3, pan: -0.5 });
audio.tone({ freq: [440, 660, 880], duration: 0.4 });   // layered partials
audio.noise({ duration: 0.5, filter: { type: "lowpass", frequency: 800 } });
```

`tone` also takes `wave` (default `"sine"`), `attack` (`0.005`) and `pitchSlide`
(`1`). `noise` takes `type` (`"white"` | `"pink"` | `"brown"`, default
`"white"`), `attack`, `pan`, `filter` and `filterSweep`. `gain` defaults to `0.1`
on both.

### Sequencing: `delay`, not `setTimeout`

Both take `delay` — seconds before the sound starts, scheduled on the **audio
clock**. That is what builds a multi-part sound: a stinger's second note, an
explosion's double-tap.

```js
audio.tone({ freq: 392, duration: 0.12 });
audio.tone({ freq: 587, duration: 0.18, delay: 0.11 });
audio.tone({ freq: [784, 1176], duration: 0.75, delay: 0.23 });
```

Do not reach for `setTimeout` here. A timer fires on the main thread, so a busy
frame slips the note late and the sequence audibly loses time — the fault is
easy to blame on the sound design rather than the scheduling. `delay` is
sample-accurate because the whole envelope is scheduled up front.

Both are **silent no-ops** when there is no WebAudio context — they bail on
`getAudioContext() === null` rather than throwing. Neither needs the clip to be
loaded; neither goes through the file-playback path at all.

`audio.getAudioContext()` and `audio.getMasterGain()` are the escape hatches for
custom Web Audio work; both return `null` when audio is unavailable, so guard.
Connect a custom graph to the master gain rather than `ctx.destination` if you
want it to respect `setVolume` / `muteAll`.

## Effects on all game audio: reverb, echo, compressor

There is no built-in reverb, delay, distortion or compressor, and no per-clip
filter on file playback. There does not need to be one for the common case:
every buffered clip and every `tone` / `noise` passes through the master gain
on its way to the speakers, so an effect inserted **after** it applies to the
whole mix.

```js
const ctx = audio.getAudioContext();   // creates the context if needed
const master = audio.getMasterGain();
if (ctx && master) {                   // null when audio is unavailable
    const comp = ctx.createDynamicsCompressor();
    master.disconnect();               // master -> speakers becomes
    master.connect(comp);              // master -> compressor -> speakers
    comp.connect(ctx.destination);
}
```

Any Web Audio node or chain works the same way: a `ConvolverNode` with an
impulse response for reverb, a `DelayNode` with a feedback gain for echo, a
`BiquadFilterNode` for an underwater low-pass, a `WaveShaperNode` for
distortion. Do it once, at startup; the master gain lives as long as the
context.

- **`setVolume` / `muteAll` still work**, because they act on the master gain,
  which is now upstream of the effect.
- **Streamed clips are not affected.** A `stream: true` (`html5: true`) clip
  plays through an `<audio>` element and never reaches the master gain — which
  is usually the music. Preload the music buffered if it must go through the
  effect.
- **It is all or nothing.** The per-instance nodes are not public, so an effect
  on one clip only (muffling one sound behind a wall) is not possible through
  this route; `noise` has its own `filter` for generated sounds.
- To remove it, reverse the wiring: `master.disconnect(); master.connect(ctx.destination);`.

## Autoplay: sound is silent until the first gesture

Browsers create the audio context in the `suspended` state and keep it there
until a user interaction. Nothing errors — audio simply does not play, which
reads as a bug. melonJS installs one-shot `touchstart` / `touchend` / `click` /
`keydown` unlock listeners on `document`, so the first real gesture anywhere
unlocks it and fires the clip's `on.unlock` callback. Design for it: start music
on the first click or key press, not on load. The usual way to guarantee one is
a gate screen — a splash, a "press any key", or a health/photosensitivity notice
— whose dismissal *is* the gesture, so the menu behind it can start its music
unconditionally. Note the unlock listens for `keydown` too, so a keyboard-only
player is covered.

Where there is no DOM (nx.js on the Nintendo Switch, see `melonjs-deployment`)
there is no page to gesture at and no autoplay policy: audio unlocks as soon as
the engine has its context, and music can start on load. nx.js's Web Audio has
buffer sources, gain and stereo panning, but not the `PannerNode`,
`OscillatorNode` and `BiquadFilterNode` behind 3D `position()` / `panner()` and
`tone()` / `noise()`, nor the reverb, echo and compressor nodes: those throw
"Method not implemented" there.

### The context can stop again, long after it was unlocked

Unlocking is only the first half. A context that has been running can be
stopped later: melonJS suspends it itself after thirty idle seconds to save
power, and browsers stop it for their own reasons, a backgrounded tab among
them. Recovery is automatic and you do not have to write it: a user gesture
or the tab coming back to the front revives it, and a deliberate idle
suspension is left alone so the power saving still works.

**The symptom worth memorising**, because it points straight at the cause:
if `tone` and `noise` are audible while loaded clips are silent, the context
is healthy and the engine's playback state is wrong. The generators only need
a live context, where a clip goes through the engine's state machine and can
be parked waiting for a resume. It is never "the context died".

Both routes ask the same owner to resume, so hearing a tone tells you the
hardware is back; it tells you nothing about whether the clips waiting on the
engine's state have been let go.

That asymmetry was a real Safari-only bug: thirty idle seconds before the
first click left the engine waiting on a suspend the browser never confirmed,
so every clip queued for the life of the page while generated sound played
normally. Fixed in 20.9, and the lesson generalises: a clip that will not play
is a state question, not a hardware one.

Playback also starts **asynchronously**: `play()` returns an id while the
instance is still starting, so `playing()` can legitimately be `false` on the
very next line.

## Load-time options

```js
{ name: "sfx", type: "audio", src: "data/sfx/",
  sprite: { jump: [0, 450] },
  pool: 5,            // finished instances kept for reuse — NOT a concurrency cap
  rate: 1.0,          // initial playback rate, 0.5..4.0
  mute: false,
  loop: false,
  autoplay: false,
  preload: true,      // false: fetched on first play, then streamed; or "metadata"
  format: "mp3",      // explicit hint when the URL has no usable extension
  stream: true,       // long music: stream rather than decode into memory
  on: { play() {}, end() {}, stop() {}, unlock() {} },
}
```

`pool` (default `5`) is a **reuse cap on finished voices**, not a limit on
simultaneous playback: when the number of ended voices exceeds it, the surplus
are disconnected and dropped. Raise it for a clip triggered in rapid bursts, not
to allow more overlap.

Use `stream: true` for long music tracks — it plays through an HTML5 `<audio>`
element instead of decoding the whole file into memory. (`html5: true` is the
same switch under its backend name.) `on` accepts the full lifecycle set:
`play`, `pause`, `stop`, `end`, `fade`, `seek`, `rate`, `volume`, `mute`,
`unlock`.

**`preload: false` keeps a clip out of the preload.** Nothing is downloaded for
it until it is first played (`audio.play`, `audio.playTrack`, or `autoplay`).
That play fetches it and streams it, as `stream: true` does, so the sound starts
as soon as enough of the file has arrived, not once all of it has; a clip never
played is never downloaded. Use it for music a player may never reach (a boss
theme, the ending) to shorten the wait before the game starts.

- The loader reports such a clip done at once: `audio.state(name)` is
  `"unloaded"` until its first play, then `"loading"`, then `"loaded"`.
- It starts with the short delay of a stream on its first play. Keep a sound
  effect that must sound the instant it is triggered preloaded.
- Being streamed, it has the limits of `stream: true`: positional sound does
  not apply to it, and it ignores `withCredentials` (see below).
- Before 20.12.0 such a clip was never fetched at all, and stayed silent.

`stream: true` alone still fetches the clip during the preload; combine it with
`preload: false` to defer that too. `preload: "metadata"` only matters for a
streamed clip: the preload fetches just enough to know its duration.

Outside a preload, `audio.load(asset, onload?, onerror?)` takes the same
descriptor and loads one clip at runtime — for a level's sounds fetched when
the level starts. The loader calls the same function, so the same rules apply.

Re-preloading a manifest that already contains a loaded clip is a no-op —
`audio.unload(name)` first if you genuinely want to reload it.

**Credentials work as for every other asset type.** Buffered audio on the
game's own origin carries its cookies and HTTP auth with no option; a clip on
another origin behind a login needs `loader.setOptions({ withCredentials: true })`,
not an audio-specific option, and that server must allow credentials. Buffered
audio fetches through the shared loader path, so it behaves exactly as an image
or a JSON file does. A streamed clip (`stream: true`, or
`preload: false`) does not: it plays
through an `<audio>` element, which needs a `crossorigin` attribute rather than
fetch credentials. Preload a clip buffered if it sits behind a login.

**Failing clips and `setStopOnAudioError(false)`.** The default is to fail the
preload when a clip cannot be loaded after its retries: the error reaches the
loader, so `await loader.preload(...)` rejects and your `catch` runs, and the
reason is logged. Turn the flag off and the engine mutes audio, warns
(`failed loading <name>, disabling audio`) and lets the load *continue* — the
preload finishes and the game reaches the next scene without sound.

Before 20.4 both halves were broken: with the flag off it disabled audio and
failed the preload anyway, and a clip whose bytes arrived but would not decode
(a missing file served as HTML by an SPA rewrite, say) reported nothing at all
either way — blank screen, empty console.

## Symptom → cause

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| audio assets 404 | `src` given as a full filename instead of a directory prefix |
| `preload()` rejects with `Failed loading resource data/sfx/` (or `audio.load()` throws `target audio extension(s) should be set...`) | `audio.init()` not called before preloading |
| `audio clip X does not exist` | the clip was never preloaded, or the name is mis-cased — every per-clip call throws this |
| "Method not implemented" from `position()`, `panner()`, `tone()`, `noise()` or an effect, on nx.js | nx.js's Web Audio lacks the node it needs (panner, oscillator, filter, convolver...): use `stereo()` and recorded sounds there |
| nothing plays until the user clicks | browser autoplay policy — expected, design around it |
| `playing()` is false right after `play()` | playback starts asynchronously |
| music keeps playing after leaving a scene | used `play` instead of `playTrack`, or no `stopTrack` in teardown |
| two music tracks playing at once, and `stopTrack()` only silences one | melonJS before 20.9.0: `playTrack` did not stop the previous track, so the scene that started it had to `stopTrack()` on the way out |
| the music restarts when returning to a screen | `playTrack` with the track already playing restarts it; don't call it again if the bed should carry on |
| `stereo` / `position` do nothing | the clip was loaded with `stream: true` or `preload: false` — spatial is WebAudio-only |
| a `preload: false` clip never plays, and `audio.state()` stays `"unloaded"` | melonJS before 20.12.0 never fetched such a clip; preload it, or update |
| one format works, another does not | that codec is not in the `audio.init()` list |
| audio on another origin behind a login fails, or the preload hangs | `loader.setOptions({ withCredentials: true })` — the same switch every asset type uses. Audio on the game's own origin needs nothing (before 20.13 it needed it too) |
| a streamed clip ignores `withCredentials` | `stream: true` plays through an `<audio>` element; preload it buffered instead |
| `audio.tone(440, {...})` does nothing / errors | `tone` takes a single options object with a required `duration` |
| `tone` / `noise` are silent with no error | no WebAudio context — `getAudioContext()` returned `null` |
| a positioned sound is silent, or only audible right next to the player | placed by hand with `audio.position()`, which keeps WebAudio's metre defaults (`refDistance: 1`) — use `follow` / `at`, or set `refDistance` in pixels with `audio.panner()` |
| a positioned sound does not follow the player | nothing is placing it — `audio.play(name, { follow: entity })`, and `audio.setListener(player)` once |
| a followed sound pans to the wrong side as the player moves | the listener was moved **and** positions are still relative to the player — with a listener in the world, pass absolute world coordinates |
| with `audio.setListener(app.viewport)`, a sound in the middle of the screen is heard off to the right (before 20.12) | the ear was at the camera's top-left corner: update, it is at the center of the view |
| a followed `Entity` (or Tiled object) sounds offset up and to the left | `follow` uses the anchor point, which is the top-left corner under their `(0, 0)` anchor |
| a looping sound outlives the entity that owns it | `follow` without `stopWithTarget: true`; with it, before 20.14 a pooled entity going back to its pool did not count either |
| new sounds are quieter than the volume slider says, or the music stays silent after the volume went to 0 and back (before 20.14) | the global volume was applied twice: update |
| "Retry" from a pause menu restarts the level with no music (before 20.14) | `playTrack` on a paused track stopped it: update |
| a clip's load-time `on: { end }` stops firing after `audio.stop(name)` (before 20.14) | `stop(name)` removed it: update |
| a voice panned with `stereo()` loses its 3D placement, or the reverse | one panner node per voice and last writer wins — pick one per voice and stay with it |
| a reverb / compressor on the master gain does not affect the music | the music is `stream: true`, which bypasses the master gain — preload it buffered |
| a looping MP3 drops out for a moment at every loop, in Safari only | Safari keeps the encoder's padding at the end of the file: loop a sprite region of the clip's exact length (see "A loop with no gap") |
| sound effects keep playing after the window loses focus | `pauseOnBlur` and `stopOnBlur` are both off, so the engine is deliberately leaving the game running in the background |
| the game still pauses and goes quiet on blur although `pauseOnBlur: false` was passed to `new Application()` | it is not a setting: assign `app.pauseOnBlur = false` |

# Camera and immediate-mode drawing

## Following a target

```js
app.viewport.follow(player, app.viewport.AXIS.BOTH, 0.1);
```

**Pass the renderable, not `renderable.pos`.** `follow()` accepts a `Renderable`,
a `Vector2d` or a `Vector3d` and **throws** `invalid target for me.Camera2d.follow`
for anything else. A renderable's `pos` is an `ObservableVector3d`, which is not
a `Vector3d` subclass, so `follow(player.pos, …)` throws.

The third argument is a damping factor in `[0 .. 1]` — lower is smoother and
laggier, `1` snaps. Omit it for a hard lock (it defaults to `1`). It is
frame-rate independent since 19.7. `AXIS.HORIZONTAL` / `AXIS.VERTICAL` /
`AXIS.BOTH` / `AXIS.NONE`.

Call it from the followed entity's `onActivateEvent`, using `this.parentApp`.

**To frame the target off centre, set `offset`; do not follow a helper
object.** It shifts the view without moving the camera, in world units, and is
applied after following and the bounds, so the view can show past them:

```js
app.viewport.follow(player, app.viewport.AXIS.BOTH, 0.1);
app.viewport.offset.set(0, -70);   // look a little above the feet

// or ahead of where the player faces, eased (see math.damp below)
const ahead = facingLeft ? -80 : 80;
app.viewport.offset.x = math.damp(app.viewport.offset.x, ahead, 4, dt / 1000);
```

Culling, tile layers, parallax `ImageLayer`s, lights and the pointer
(`localToWorld`, `worldToLocal`) all count it. `shake()` adds its jitter on top
and gives the value back when it ends, so setting it before or during a shake
is fine. `reset()` clears it.

**For anything that is NOT the camera, the same smoothing is `math.damp`.**
`follow()` is frame-rate independent for you; a value you smooth yourself is
not, and `lerp(current, target, alpha)` once per frame moves further on a slow
frame than on a fast one, so the feel changes with the frame rate:

```js
import { math } from "melonjs";

// dt is milliseconds, damp wants seconds
this.speed = math.damp(this.speed, targetSpeed, 5, dt / 1000);
this.turret.angle = math.damp(this.turret.angle, wanted, 8, dt / 1000);
```

`damp(current, target, lambda, dt)`. Higher `lambda` converges faster; it is
the rate, not a per-frame fraction.

**For a DIRECTION rather than a scalar, the tool is `slerp`**, on `Vector2d`
and `Vector3d` alike. Two reasons, and the second is the one that bites:

```js
// a turret, a ship, a camera: a facing that chases another facing
facing.slerp(toTarget, 1 - Math.exp((-6 * dt) / 1000));
```

1. Damping a facing component by component drags it through the inside of the
   circle, so it slows at the ends, rushes the middle and comes out shorter
   than it went in.
2. **Damping a scalar heading goes the wrong way round the wrap.** From 170
   degrees to -170 degrees is 20 degrees apart, and the numbers are 340 apart,
   so the turret sweeps all the way round the back. `slerp` works on the
   directions, takes the shorter arc by construction, and has no wrap to cross.

See `melonjs-3d` for the rest, including what happens between two exactly
opposite directions. Use it for camera pans you drive yourself,
turret tracking, zoom, input smoothing and any value that should chase another
one — it is the tool that is easy to miss and easy to hand-write slightly
wrong.

## Bounds are the thing people forget

The camera's bounds default to the **renderer size**, so it cannot scroll until
you widen them to the world:

```js
app.viewport.setBounds(0, 0, mapWidth, mapHeight);
```

Symptom: `follow()` is called, looks right, and the view never moves. Note a
canvas resize resets the default camera's bounds to `(0, 0, w, h)`, so re-apply
them from a `CANVAS_ONRESIZE` handler if your game resizes. Loading a Tiled map
sets them for you from the map size.

## Camera effects

```js
app.viewport.shake(4, 200);                       // intensity, ms
app.viewport.fadeIn("#000000", 500);              // fade TO black
app.viewport.fadeOut("#000000", 500);             // start black, fade back to normal
app.viewport.colorMatrix.contrast(1.1).saturate(1.1);
app.viewport.addPostEffect(new VignetteEffect(app.renderer));
```

The fade pair is named from the *colour's* point of view, not the scene's:
`fadeIn` fades the colour in (screen goes to `color`), `fadeOut` fades it out
(screen starts at `color` and clears). Both default to a 1000 ms duration and
take an optional completion callback.

`shake()` while a shake is still running is ignored, unless its fifth
argument, `force`, is `true`, which replaces the running one:

```js
app.viewport.shake(8, 300, app.viewport.AXIS.BOTH, undefined, true);
```

**`fadeIn` does not HOLD the colour.** The effect completes, the camera's own
update destroys it, and the screen snaps back — which is why the engine's
idiom does the work in the completion callback and then calls `fadeOut`. To
keep a filled screen across a state change, own the effect: a completed one
marked `isPersistent` is left alone, and taking it away again is yours to do.

```js
const hide = camera.addCameraEffect(
    new FadeEffect(camera, { color: "#000", duration: 400, direction: "in" }),
);
hide.isPersistent = true;          // survives completion AND Camera2d#reset()
// ... later, once the new stage is up
camera.removeCameraEffect(hide);   // which destroys it for you
```

That is exactly what `state.transition()` is built on, so a hand-rolled
transition behaves the same way. Before 20.9 a persistent effect was destroyed
on completion like any other, which is why a transition used to flash the
scene it had just covered.

`colorMatrix` (`brightness` / `contrast` / `saturate` / `hueRotate` / `sepia` /
`invertColors`, all chainable) is the cheap way to grade a whole camera: the
camera appends it as a final post-effect pass by itself whenever the matrix is
non-identity, and drops it again after the frame. It is **not** shader-free —
it is a `ColorMatrixEffect`, i.e. a `ShaderEffect`, so like every post effect it
is inert on the Canvas renderer.

### The camera effects, and your own

Each is a `CameraEffect`, added with `camera.addCameraEffect(effect)` (which
returns it), found with `getCameraEffect(Class)` and taken off with
`removeCameraEffect(effect)`, which destroys it:

| effect | options | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `ShakeEffect` | `intensity`, `duration`, `axis`, `onComplete` | jitters `offset`; what `shake()` adds. Several can run at once this way |
| `FadeEffect` | `color`, `duration` (1000), `direction: "in" \| "out"`, `onComplete` | what `fadeIn()` / `fadeOut()` add |
| `MaskEffect` | `shape`, `color`, `duration` (500), `direction: "hide" \| "reveal"`, `onComplete` | an iris or a wipe through a unit-sized `Ellipse` or `Polygon` centred on the origin |
| `PixelateTransitionEffect` | `renderer`, `size` (32), `duration` (500), `direction: "hide" \| "reveal"`, `onComplete` | the view breaks into blocks up to `size` screen pixels, or comes back from them. A shader: on Canvas it keeps its timing and draws nothing |

`state.transition("fade" | "mask" | "pixelate", …)` drives the last three
for a state change (see `melonjs-scenes-and-state`). A `Trigger` that loads a
level transitions only with both a `color` and a `duration`, and takes only
`transition: "fade"` (the default) or `"mask"` with a `shape`: anything else,
`"pixelate"` included, is a fade.

For an effect of your own, extend `CameraEffect`: `update(dt)` runs every
frame (`dt` in ms), `draw(renderer, width, height)` draws over the camera's
view, and `destroy()` frees what it holds. Set `isComplete = true` and the
camera's update destroys it that frame, unless it is `isPersistent`.

## Zoom and roll

```js
app.viewport.zoom = 2;              // above 1 zooms in, below 1 out
app.viewport.roll = Math.PI / 32;   // a slight dutch angle, in radians
```

A zoomed camera follows, keeps to its bounds and centres on `focusOn` in world
units, and `localToWorld` / `worldToLocal` count the zoom. A zoom of 0 or less
is taken as 1.

`roll` is absolute (assigning the same angle twice changes nothing), and the
pointer conversions undo it, so picking under a rolled camera needs nothing.
It OWNS the camera's `currentTransform`: each assignment rebuilds it, so a
`rotate()` or `scale()` called on the camera itself is lost at the next one.
`reset()` puts it back to 0. On a `Camera3d` the same `roll` banks the view
(see below).

## Coordinate conversion

```js
app.viewport.worldToLocal(x, y);   // world → screen
app.viewport.localToWorld(x, y);   // screen → world
```

They agree with where the camera draws: a level smaller than the view is
centred by offsetting the world container (`world.pos`), which the default
camera draws and a minimap, corner or zoomed camera leaves out, and each
camera's conversions follow suit (20.13 and later; before, a minimap's were off
by `world.pos`).

Both return a `Vector2d`; with no third argument that vector comes from the
shared pool, so in a per-frame path pass your own `v` as the third argument, or
release it with `getPool("vector2d").release(v)`.

Pointer events already carry every frame of reference: `gameWorldX`/`gameWorldY`
(world), `gameScreenX`/`gameScreenY` (screen), `gameLocalX`/`gameLocalY`
(relative to the registered region's container) and `gameX`/`gameY`, which is
whichever of world/screen matches the region — screen for a `floating` region,
world otherwise. Use the screen pair for anything that *moves* the camera, or
the drag feeds back on itself.

### In 3D: `Camera3d#worldToScreen`

`worldToLocal` is a 2D camera's offset subtraction — it knows nothing about a
perspective projection. To pin a label, damage number or marker to a point in a
3D scene, project it:

```js
const p = camera.worldToScreen(x, y, z);   // view + projection, divide included
if (p !== null) {                          // null = at or BEHIND the camera
    label.pos.set(p.x, p.y);
}
```

It returns canvas pixels with the origin top-left and **y down**, which is the
engine's own 2D draw space — so the result feeds a `floating` renderable or the
immediate-mode API directly, with no flip.

**Always check for `null`.** A point at or behind the camera (clip `w <= 0`)
has no honest screen position, and projecting it anyway yields a mirrored
coordinate that puts your label on the wrong side of the screen. Skip it.

Do not hand-roll this with `Matrix3d` — the perspective divide and the behind-
camera case are exactly what gets it wrong.

## Pointing a 3D camera

A 2D camera's only rotation is `roll`. A 3D one can be pointed at a target, and
optionally banked at the same time:

```js
camera.lookAt(target);                  // pitch and yaw; roll untouched
camera.lookAt(target, up);              // and bank, where `up` is what should
                                        // appear UP ON SCREEN
camera.setBasis(right, up, forward);    // or pose it from a basis outright
```

`up` has no default, so the one-argument form behaves exactly as it always
did. Because this engine renders Y-down, a level horizon is `(0, -1, 0)`.
`setBasis` is the writable counterpart of `getBasis` and takes the camera's
own columns, whose `up` points down the screen: the opposite sense, one
negation apart. See `melonjs-3d` for the full account.

## Secondary cameras

Cameras are first-class — a minimap is a second camera with `autoResize = false`
and an overridden `postDraw`:

```js
this.cameras.set("minimap", new MinimapCamera());
```

A stage's cameras draw in the order they were added, each over the ones before
it, so a full-screen second camera is a layer: a `Camera3d` drawing a 3D
background first, the game's own camera over it, each kept to its part of the
world with `visibilityLayer` / `cullMask` (below). A camera's post effects
apply to what that camera draws: the first camera's pass starts the frame, and
a later camera's is blended over what is already there (20.13 and later;
before, it wiped out the cameras before it).

View state is per camera, not per scene: a `Camera3d` carries its own distance
fog (`setFog`), so a minimap or split-screen view fogs independently of the main
one — and a `Camera2d` never fogs. See `melonjs-3d`.

### What each camera draws: `visibilityLayer` and `cullMask`

Every camera draws the whole world. To keep something off one camera only, put
it on a layer that camera leaves out. A renderable's `visibilityLayer` is the
layers it is on, as bits (1, 2, 4...); a camera's `cullMask` is the layers it
draws. A camera draws a renderable only if the two share a bit:

```js
const PARTICLES = 2;
emitter.visibilityLayer = PARTICLES;   // the particles go on layer 2
minimap.cullMask = ~PARTICLES;         // the minimap draws every layer but 2
```

- By default every renderable is on layer 1 and every camera draws every layer
  (`cullMask` is `-1`), so nothing changes until a game sets one.
- A container left out is left out with everything inside it, however deep:
  set it on an emitter and none of its particles are drawn. The world itself
  obeys it too, and so does what it contains: a child is drawn only if it and
  every container above it share a bit with the camera.
- Particles are on their emitter's layers, and follow a change to them on the
  emitter's next update, so a camera that draws only the emitter's layer draws
  its particles too.
- A renderable on layer `0` is drawn by no camera; a `cullMask` of `0` draws
  nothing.
- It decides drawing only: what a camera leaves out still updates, collides and
  receives pointer events.
- A `Light2d` a camera leaves out, itself or a container it is in, neither
  glows, nor cuts its hole in the darkness, nor lights normal-mapped sprites in
  that camera. A `Light3d` lights the meshes of every camera.
- It adds to the floating rule: a floating renderable is drawn by a secondary
  camera only with `visibleInAllCameras`, and only if the layers match as well.
- On a Tiled object, set it as an `int` custom property named
  `visibilityLayer`.

## Immediate-mode drawing

Inside a custom `draw(renderer)` you can draw shapes directly. Remember the two
renderable rules: read `this.pos`, and zero the anchor.

```js
draw(renderer) {
    renderer.setColor("#ff8800");
    renderer.fillRect(this.pos.x, this.pos.y, this.width, this.height);

    renderer.setColor("#ffffff");
    renderer.lineWidth = 2;                 // property, not setLineWidth()
    renderer.stroke(new Line(0, 0, [/* … */]));
}
```

**The colour's alpha and the global alpha are two things**, as on a 2D
context. A fill or a stroke is drawn at the alpha of `setColor` times
`setGlobalAlpha` (which is where the renderable's opacity comes in), an image at
the global alpha (times the tint) alone, and `getGlobalAlpha()` never moves with
`setColor`. So to fade a translucent shape, lower the global alpha and keep the
colour; folding the colour's alpha into `setGlobalAlpha` as well counts it twice.

`lineWidth`, `lineJoin`, the colour and the global alpha are all part of what
`save()` / `restore()` keep, and every renderable's `draw()` runs between the
two, so set them freely there: the next renderable gets them back.

`fillArc` / `strokeArc` read their angles like `CanvasRenderingContext2D.arc`:
an end before the start wraps round (`end + 2π`), and a span of 2π or more in
the arc's own direction is the whole circle. A filled part-circle differs by
backend, though: Canvas closes it with a straight chord, the GPU renderers fill
a pie slice from the centre.

Geometry available: `Rect`, `RoundRect`, `Ellipse`, `Polygon`, `Line`, `Point`
(and a `Bounds`), plus the 3D `Box3d` and `Sphere`, drawn as their footprint
and their circle on the screen plane. `renderer.fill(shape)` and
`renderer.stroke(shape)` take any of them and throw `Invalid geometry for
fill/stroke` for anything else.

### Paths and SVG strings

For any other outline, build a path on the renderer's own `renderer.path2D`,
then call `fill()` / `stroke()` with no argument:

```js
renderer.path2D.parseSVGPath("M 50 0 L 100 100 L 0 100 Z");
renderer.setColor("#4CAF50");
renderer.fill();
```

`renderer.path2D` also takes the methods of the browser's `Path2D`
(`beginPath`, `moveTo`, `lineTo`, `arc`, `arcTo`, `ellipse`, `rect`,
`roundRect`, `quadraticCurveTo`, `bezierCurveTo`, `closePath`).

- **Every `moveTo`, every `M`, starts a sub-path, and filled, each one after
  the first is a HOLE**: a donut, the counter of an "O". Wind a hole the
  opposite way to the outline, as Canvas fills by the non-zero rule, where a
  hole wound the same way fills in. Draw separate shapes with separate fills.
- **`parseSVGPath` reads absolute commands only** (`M L H V Q C A Z`). A
  lowercase, relative command is read as its absolute twin, so a path
  exported with relative commands comes out scrambled, and `H` / `V` take an
  OFFSET from the pen, not the coordinate SVG means. Export absolute
  coordinates.
- **The engine's `Path2D` class is not exported.** `new Path2D()` in a game is
  the browser's own, which `fill()` / `stroke()` refuse as invalid geometry:
  use `renderer.path2D`.

`Gradient` gives linear and radial fills, built with
`renderer.createLinearGradient(x0, y0, x1, y1)` /
`createRadialGradient(x0, y0, r0, x1, y1, r1)` and then handed to
`renderer.setColor(gradient)`. `NoiseTexture2d` generates cellular and simplex
noise — including seamless tiling and `asNormalMap` — so you rarely need to ship
noise PNGs.

Two things to get right when one is animated:

- **Drive it yourself.** `update(dt)` advances the time axis and re-bakes; the
  engine never calls it. An `animated: true` texture nobody updates is a still
  image, with no error to say so.
- **Hand consumers the texture, not its canvas.** Re-baking bumps the
  `Texture2d`'s `version`, and that bump is what tells the renderer to
  re-upload. `getTexture()` returns the baked canvas, which carries no version
  — so a mesh given the canvas shows frame one forever.

Set `seamless: true` for anything tiled by UVs past 1, or every repeat carries a
visible seam.

**And it still will not animate on a `Mesh`.** Driving `update(dt)` genuinely
re-bakes the field — the pixels change, the version increments — but the mesh
path does not pick the new copy up, so a 3D surface textured with an animated
noise renders frozen while every counter reports success. Verify with a
checksum of `getTexture()` before concluding the animation is broken; it is the
upload that is missing, not the bake. For a moving 3D surface, scroll the UVs
or move the geometry instead.
